item.title: NetNut Botnet Disrupted as DPRK npm and EvilTokens Phishing Campaigns Target Credentials
Armored Likho BusySnake Campaign, Pegasus Hacks, and QR Code Quishing
PamStealer Targets macOS as Silent Push Details Proactive Phishing Infrastructure Hunting
Pegasus Spyware Found on European Parliament PEGA Committee Member’s Phone
phpBB CVE-2026-48611, Bad Epoll, FatFs Flaws and NetNut Disruption Lead Threats
item.content:encoded:
Authentication Bypass in the default configuration phpBB — Must Read

phpBB patched a critical default-configuration authentication bypass in version 3.3.17 that let unauthenticated attackers log in as any user, including admins, by abusing the login-link flow with the Apache auth provider. Site operators should update immediately and check logs for suspicious login_link requests using auth_provider=apache.

  • Aikido reported a critical phpBB authentication bypass, now identified as CVE-2026-48611, that works in the default configuration and requires only a single unauthenticated request to log in to an arbitrary account.
  • The vulnerability is in phpBB’s login-link flow, where an attacker can provide dummy login_link data and control the auth_provider parameter to select the apache provider.
  • The apache authentication provider trusts the Basic authentication username and returns a successful login for an existing active user without checking the submitted password, because it is intended for deployments where Apache handles authentication first.
  • phpBB triaged the HackerOne report in under 9 minutes and released a patch in version 3.3.17 four days after the report.
  • The article recommends checking request logs for POST requests combining mode=login_link, auth_provider=apache, and login_link_* parameters, including cases where mode and auth_provider are supplied in the POST body.

Armored Likho digging a snake pit: inside the covert BusySnake Stealer campaign — Must Read

Kaspersky uncovered an active Armored Likho phishing campaign targeting government and electric power organizations in Russia, Brazil, and Kazakhstan with a new Python infostealer called BusySnake Stealer. The malware uses AI-generated loaders, PyArmor obfuscation, browser credential and cookie theft, persistence via scheduled tasks, and built-in reverse SSH tunneling for stealthy access and data exfiltration.

  • Kaspersky uncovered an active phishing campaign tied to the previously unknown APT group Armored Likho, also known as Eagle Werewolf based on circumstantial evidence, targeting government agencies and the electric power sector in Russia, Brazil, and Kazakhstan.
  • The campaign uses malicious archive attachments containing EXE droppers or LNK files, including LNK files that abuse ZDI-CAN-25373 to hide command-line content and execute PowerShell-based downloaders.
  • The primary payload is BusySnake Stealer, a previously undocumented Python-based infostealer protected with PyArmor Pro 9.2.0 and designed to run on Windows without opening a console window.
  • BusySnake Stealer can steal clipboard data, documents, screenshots, browser passwords, browser cookies, 2FA secrets, cryptocurrency wallet JSON files, and Telegram session data, and it can establish reverse SSH tunnels and interact with RustDesk for remote control.
  • A newer BusySnake Stealer version creates scheduled tasks through the Windows Schedule.Service COM object, adds delayed execution to bypass dynamic analysis, and introduces a task-management framework for commands and in-memory execution of Python scripts from the C2 server.

North Korea-Linked npm Packages Mimic Rollup Polyfills to Steal Developer Secrets — Must Read

North Korea-linked actors published malicious npm packages that impersonate Rollup polyfill tooling to infect developer machines, enable remote access, and steal credentials, browser data, crypto wallets, and project secrets. Developers who installed the named packages should remove them, assume compromise, and rotate exposed credentials.

  • JFrog linked North Korea-tied threat actors to malicious npm packages named rollup-packages-polyfill-core and rollup-runtime-polyfill-core that mimic the legitimate rollup-plugin-polyfill-node project.
  • The campaign also involved quirky-token, react-icon-svgs, rollup-plugin-polyfill-connect, and swift-parse-stream, all of which have been removed from the npm registry.
  • The first-stage packages concealed Base64-encoded npm install commands for second-stage packages, which fetched a JSON object from JSONKeeper and executed JavaScript from its model field.
  • The malware checked for cloud development environments, sandboxes, serverless runtimes, and analysis infrastructure before fetching an encrypted JavaScript payload from 216.126.236[.]244.
  • Later payload stages enabled remote terminal sessions, command execution, screenshot capture, input control, browser and cryptocurrency wallet data theft, file collection, and periodic clipboard capture.

New "Bad Epoll" Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Unprivileged Users Gain Root, Hits Android — Should Read

A new Linux kernel flaw called Bad Epoll lets unprivileged users gain root on affected Linux 6.4+ systems and may also impact Android, with a fix now available. There is no workaround, so users and admins should apply the upstream patch or distribution backport as soon as possible.

  • Bad Epoll, tracked as CVE-2026-46242, is a newly disclosed Linux kernel flaw that can let an unprivileged user gain root access on affected systems.
  • The flaw is a use-after-free bug in epoll where two kernel cleanup paths can collide, allowing memory corruption if an attacker wins a very small timing window.
  • Jaeyoung Chung found the flaw, built a working exploit, and reported it through Google's kernelCTF program, with tested systems reaching root about 99% of the time.
  • Kernels built on Linux 6.4 or newer are affected unless they already include the fix, while older 6.1-based kernels such as some Android phones including the Pixel 8 are not affected.
  • There is no workaround because epoll cannot be turned off, so users must apply upstream commit a6dc643c6931 or install their distribution's backport when available.

Unpatched Flaws Disclosed in Filesystem Bundled Into Millions of Embedded Devices — Should Read

runZero disclosed seven mostly unpatched FatFs vulnerabilities affecting millions of embedded devices that read FAT/exFAT media, with some flaws enabling memory corruption and possible code execution via malicious USB drives, SD cards, or update files. With no upstream fixes for the most serious bugs, device vendors must patch downstream and users should treat physical media ports and firmware update channels as exposed attack surfaces.

  • runZero disclosed seven vulnerabilities in FatFs, a small filesystem library used by embedded devices to read and write FAT and exFAT formats on USB drives and SD cards.
  • The most severe flaws can allow an attacker to use a malformed USB drive, SD card, or update file to corrupt memory and potentially run code on affected devices.
  • FatFs is bundled in firmware for devices including security cameras, drones, industrial controllers, hardware crypto wallets, and products built on real-time operating systems.
  • Only CVE-2026-6684, a malformed GPT partition table issue that can hang a device during mount, is fixed upstream in FatFs R0.16.
  • runZero said it could not reach the FatFs maintainer despite repeated attempts and named affected platforms including Espressif ESP-IDF, STMicroelectronics STM32Cube, Zephyr, MicroPython, ArduPilot, RT-Thread, Mbed, Samsung TizenRT, and SWUpdate.

New Avalon Malware Framework Packs CrownX Ransomware Capabilities — Should Read

Researchers found a new modular malware framework called Avalon that uses a phishing chain to steal credentials, evade defenses, move laterally, disrupt recovery, and deploy its CrownX ransomware component. The report also highlights a broader trend of AI lowering the barrier for ransomware and malware development, including agentic and LLM-assisted attacks.

  • Cybersecurity researchers discovered a previously undocumented modular malware framework called Avalon that is distributed through a multi-stage phishing chain using a spoofed legal document email and a password-protected Proton Drive archive.
  • Avalon combines credential collection, lateral movement, remote access, recovery disruption, and ransomware execution, with its ransomware component internally named CrownX.
  • The attack chain uses a Windows Shortcut inside an ISO image to launch an MSBuild project, which loads an embedded .NET assembly, interferes with Event Tracing for Windows, and downloads a next-stage payload over HTTPS to launch Avalon.
  • Avalon includes defense evasion capabilities aimed at security tools associated with Microsoft Defender, SentinelOne, CrowdStrike, Sophos, Elastic Endpoint, FortiEDR, ESET, McAfee, and Bitdefender.
  • The article says Avalon shows signs of AI-assisted development and presents this as evidence that AI can lower the barrier to creating malware and ransomware tools.

NetNut proxy network disrupted, 2 million infected devices cut off — Should Read

Google, the FBI, and industry partners disrupted NetNut, a major residential proxy botnet that routed malicious traffic through at least 2 million compromised Android devices, smart TVs, and streaming boxes. The operation seized domains, cut off command-and-control infrastructure, and disabled infected apps via Google Play Protect.

  • A joint operation involving Google disrupted NetNut, also known as Popa, a residential proxy network estimated to control at least 2 million compromised devices globally, including Android devices, smart TVs, and streaming boxes.
  • Google said NetNut was powered by trojanized applications and botnets such as Badbox 2.0 that package proxy plugins.
  • The disruption involved Google, the FBI, Lumen Technologies, The Shadowserver Foundation, and other industry partners, and the FBI took down domains including netnut.com.
  • Google observed 316 distinct threat clusters using suspected NetNut exit nodes in one week last month, including cybercriminal and espionage groups.
  • Google disabled accounts and services used by NetNut operators for command-and-control infrastructure and protected users by warning them and disabling infected applications through Google Play Protect.

ARToken PhaaS exposes EvilTokens' Microsoft 365 phishing toolkit — Should Read

Cisco Talos uncovered ARToken, a phishing-as-a-service panel linked to EvilTokens that helps attackers compromise Microsoft 365 accounts through device code phishing, steal tokens, maintain persistent access, and automate BEC activity. The findings show EvilTokens affiliates have a broad toolkit for bypassing MFA and abusing Outlook, SharePoint, and OneDrive after account takeover.

  • Cisco Talos researchers discovered a React-based management panel called ARToken Panel that exposed more than 80 API endpoints while investigating phishing infrastructure used in an incident response engagement.
  • Talos found multiple technical similarities suggesting ARToken is tied to the EvilTokens phishing platform, including identical Microsoft device code authentication API calls and the same primary refresh token API endpoints documented in prior EvilTokens research.
  • ARToken allows attackers to steal Microsoft 365 authentication tokens, establish persistent access using Primary Refresh Tokens, and access Outlook mailboxes, SharePoint sites, and OneDrive files.
  • The platform includes tools for business email compromise operations, such as sending emails as compromised users, creating inbox rules to forward or hide messages, monitoring mailboxes for keywords, and downloading email attachments.
  • Phishing emails associated with the platform impersonated legitimate vendors in invoice-themed lures targeting accounts payable employees and displayed what appeared to be a legitimate SharePoint address while redirecting victims to an attacker-controlled Microsoft 365 tenant.

European Parliament Member Investigating Spyware Was Hacked With Pegasus — Should Read

Citizen Lab found that former European Parliament member Stelios Kouloglou was repeatedly infected with NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware while serving on the PEGA committee investigating spyware abuse. The attacks may have exposed confidential committee work and suggest a Pegasus operator licensed to target across multiple EU countries.

  • Citizen Lab reported that former Member of the European Parliament Stelios Kouloglou had his mobile device repeatedly hacked with Pegasus spyware while serving on the PEGA Committee investigating the use of Pegasus and similar surveillance tools.
  • Forensic analysis found Pegasus compromises on or around October 21, 2022, and again on March 6 and 7, 2023, while Kouloglou’s device was running iOS 15.5.
  • Citizen Lab assessed that the attacks used the PWNYOURHOME zero-click exploit in Apple’s HomeKit software, which Apple addressed in iOS 16.3.1.
  • Citizen Lab said the infections have not been attributed to a particular government and that there is no evidence the Greek government was behind the activity.
  • Citizen Lab identified an overlap between the first infection and a previous campaign targeting Russian and Belarusian-speaking exiled journalists and activists in Europe through the same email address, rauharepo888@gmail.com.

PamStealer Uses Fake Maccy Sites and PAM Checks to Steal Mac Login Passwords — Should Read

Researchers found a new macOS infostealer, PamStealer, spread through fake Maccy websites that tricks users into running a malicious AppleScript and then steals passwords, browser data, crypto wallet data, iCloud Keychain content, and clipboard contents. Its key tactic is validating the victim’s macOS login password locally through PAM before exfiltrating data, making the credential theft more reliable and stealthy.

  • Jamf Threat Labs discovered a new macOS information stealer called PamStealer that is distributed as a compiled AppleScript file impersonating the legitimate open-source clipboard manager Maccy.
  • PamStealer is delivered through a lookalike website, maccyapp.com, that mimics the official Maccy website at maccy.app.
  • The malware uses a two-stage chain in which an AppleScript inside a disk image downloads a Rust-based information stealer capable of credential theft, browser data collection, persistence, and exfiltration.
  • The AppleScript dropper only continues after fingerprinting the host, including CPU architecture, locale, keyboard layout, and time zone, and it avoids Intel-based Macs, sandboxed or analysis environments, and systems associated with several Eastern European countries.
  • The Rust payload steals data from web browsers, cryptocurrency wallet extensions, iCloud Keychain, and clipboard content, and it uses a native password prompt to capture and validate the victim’s macOS login password through the PAM API.

The Payroll Memo Whose Link You Could Not Scan: QR Code Quishing Buried in a Word Attachment — Should Read

Attackers sent a personalized payroll-themed Word attachment containing an embedded QR code that led to a credential-harvesting site, bypassing normal email URL scanning because the link existed only as an image. The key lesson is that defenses must inspect attachments for QR codes and combine that with context like failed SPF/DKIM/DMARC and self-addressed sender abuse.

  • A procurement employee received a blank email with a Word attachment named Revised_Pay_Structure_Notice.docx that appeared to be an HR salary-update memo.
  • The DOCX contained an embedded PNG QR code that decoded to a credential-harvesting URL, with no clickable link in the email body for inline scanners to inspect.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all failed, and the sender address was the recipient's own address.
  • The document used the recipient's full name and email address, referenced the next payroll cycle, and claimed to provide updated compensation details to build trust.
  • The article says detection should decode QR codes inside documents, evaluate the resulting destination, and weigh context such as failed authentication and self-addressed messages.

Claude Fable relaunch disappoints users with nerfed performance — May Read

Anthropic’s restored Claude Fable 5 is available to more users but is heavily capped and often falls back to Opus 4.8 due to strict safety guardrails. Users say the result feels significantly weaker than the original release, especially for coding and security-adjacent tasks.

  • Claude Fable 5 is now available to all users, including Max, Pro, and Team subscribers, but Anthropic says it is heavily capped.
  • Anthropic says users can use Fable for up to 50% of their weekly usage limits, and after July 7 the model will transition entirely to a usage-credits system.
  • Users on Reddit report that the restored Fable 5 feels weaker or is routed through stricter safety systems more often than before.
  • Claude Code users report that tasks involving C, C++, Rust, Win32 API references, memory-related work, or words like “security,” “vulnerable,” “unsafe,” and “hook” can trigger a fallback or block.
  • BleepingComputer says the model itself has likely not been nerfed, but Anthropic’s extra safety guardrails and large safety margin are negatively affecting daily use cases.

Powerful Pivots: From a Single Phish to a Full Campaign — Optional

A single phishing email can be used as a starting point to proactively uncover a broader campaign by pivoting from clues like domains, page titles, WHOIS data, and registrar patterns. The article shows how defenders can hunt for related Ledger-themed phishing infrastructure before it is used in attacks.

  • The investigation starts with email headers from a real-world Ledger phishing email.
  • The article identifies IPs including 149.72.223.116 and 159.183.183.61 as indicators of compromised SendGrid accounts.
  • The malicious link in the phishing email was ledger-recovery-app.com.
  • The article describes pivoting from the domain to find other sites with an HTML title of “Are you human?” and a URL containing “ledger.”
  • The article proposes a proactive domain and WHOIS query for domains matching ledger-*-*.com or *-ledger-*.com registered through Amazon Registrar, Inc.

Powerful Pivots: Hunting with Infrastructure Fingerprints — Optional

The article shows how defenders can pivot on infrastructure fingerprints like HTTP Hash and JARM to find related phishing domains even when the content and domain names change. Using these fingerprints can reveal high-confidence phishing sites such as gmaii.email while avoiding legitimate infrastructure.

  • The article says threat actors often reuse the same server configurations across different campaigns.
  • A phishing domain, harborfrieght[.]shop, was identified as the example for extracting server technical signatures.
  • The article identifies HHV f2bbb45599ecd7349b164c98a8 and JARM 27d40d40d00040d00042d43d00041df04c41293ba84f6efe3a613b22f983e6 as key indicators to pivot on.
  • The goal is to query for all domains hosted on infrastructure with the exact same HHV and JARM fingerprints.
  • The article says this multi-layered search identifies high-fidelity phishing sites such as gmaii.email while ignoring legitimate Google infrastructure.

Powerful Pivots: Uncovering Brand Impersonation with Multi-Layered Queries — Optional

Silent Push describes a multi-layered search technique for finding Gmail impersonation sites by combining favicon hashes, page titles, and SSL issuer filtering. The key takeaway is that excluding certificates issued by Google Trust Services helps separate convincing phishing clones from legitimate Google infrastructure.

  • The article states that proactively finding convincing clones of a major brand like Gmail is difficult because many legitimate and benign sites use the word “gmail.”
  • The article describes a multi-layered query that combines several data points to filter out noise when searching for fake Gmail-related sites.
  • The search logic starts by finding all sites using the official Gmail favicon hash and then adds a condition that the HTML title must contain “gmail.”
  • The article says the most important step is excluding any site where the SSL Issuer Organization is “Google Trust Services,” because that would indicate a real Google-owned property.
  • The article says this search can identify high-fidelity phishing sites such as gmaii.email while ignoring legitimate Google infrastructure.

Staying "Left of Boom" with Preemptive Cyber Defense — Optional

Silent Push’s Zach Edwards explains how security teams can stay ahead of attacks by monitoring static and changing infrastructure data to identify attacker systems before they are used. The key takeaway is that proactive tracking of DNS and infrastructure changes can provide early warning of emerging campaigns.

  • Senior Threat Researcher Zach Edwards explains how organizations can stay left of the boom with proactive cyber defense.
  • The session covers how tracking both static data and change data can help identify attacker infrastructure before it is weaponized.
  • The article says threat actors adapt to evade detection and that security teams can fingerprint attacker infrastructure to spot emerging campaigns.
  • The session discusses monitoring DNS and infrastructure changes for early warning.
  • The full session is described as essential viewing for CISOs, threat hunters, and security teams looking to stay ahead of advanced threat actors.

Get Started with Silent Push Community Edition — Optional

Silent Push is promoting its free Community Edition, which offers introductory access to its cyber defense platform and datasets for investigating relationships across internet infrastructure.

  • Silent Push Community Edition is a free cyber defense tool that provides introductory access to the Silent Push platform and datasets.
  • Researchers use Silent Push to uncover relationships between billions of Internet datapoints.
  • The tool is described as helping expose how adversaries deploy and manage their infrastructure.
  • Silent Push invites users to sign up for free and share feedback.

The Silent Push Difference — Optional

Silent Push promotes its platform as a proactive threat intelligence service that scans global internet infrastructure daily to identify attacker infrastructure before it is used. Its key pitch is replacing reactive IOCs with “Indicators of Future Attack” to help security teams block threats earlier.

  • Silent Push says the global security industry tracks only 2% of live attacker infrastructure.
  • Silent Push focuses on the remaining 98% of live attacker infrastructure to help organizations track, monitor, and counteract global cyber threats.
  • Silent Push says it scans the entire global IPv4 and IPv6 space daily to create a first-party database of internet-facing infrastructure.
  • Silent Push says it creates Indicators of Future Attack by analyzing how adversaries build and manage their infrastructure.
  • Silent Push says its approach helps security teams proactively block hidden threats before they are weaponized.

What is Traffic Origin? — Optional

Silent Push is promoting Traffic Origin, a product meant to reveal the true upstream source controlling network connections so organizations can proactively block or challenge suspicious traffic before infrastructure is weaponized.

  • Traditional security stacks are described as reactive because they identify malicious infrastructure only after it has been weaponized.
  • Silent Push Traffic Origin is presented as shifting security posture from reactive investigation to proactive validation.
  • Traffic Origin aims to unmask the true upstream source of a connection and move organizations beyond simple IP geolocation.
  • The article says Traffic Origin is built to detect upstream control signals that are invisible to traditional intelligence.
  • Traffic Origin is promoted as helping organizations pre-emptively block or challenge traffic based on where it is actually controlled.
